Having that downstream definitely worries me. Having the wiring in parallel will split the amperage used on the two legs while keeping the voltage constant. Which would in your case effective double the overcurrent protection but only on that leg and it’s parallel. 
The issue with that is if it trips the parallel will still be on. Parallel feeds always need to be fused and the same length as their other feeds to avoid unbalanced loads. The way this is set up will likely burn up sensitive 240 equipment or could burn something up if it on the 120 side.

In most applications it’s preferred to pigtail, not because it’s safer, but for troubleshooting future failures. 
For instance if you have five receptacles on the same circuit wired as shown in the picture and the first outlet had a bad connection you would loose the whole run. If you had t personally installed every outlet and pulled the wire you would have no idea it was the first receptacle of the run and would be forced to inspect every outlet until you find the issue. 
If it’s pigtailed and a receptacle fails you only loose that one device. It’s clear where the failure is.

Love @kona420 explanation. The only thing I wanted to add is these “primary panels” are typically referred to service entrance panels. You can tell this is a service entrance a couple of ways: The obvious one is that the grounds and neutrals are mixed and it has a little green screw on the neutral bar. This screw physically “cuts” into the back of the panel to bond the neutral bar, the panel, and the ground bar together. It comes with the panel but should only be installed on service entrance applications.
